relevance_reason: The title describes treating a patient with GAD1 deficiency, which is the cause of DEE89. Only the title was available, so no clinical or variant details could be extracted.

findings.statement: von Hardenberg et al. (2020) reported rational therapy with vigabatrin and a ketogenic diet in a patient with GAD1 deficiency.
quotes: Rational therapy with vigabatrin and a ketogenic diet in a patient with GAD1 deficiency.

relevance_reason: This is the original report of 6 patients from 6 unrelated families with biallelic GAD1 variants causing developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, which defines DEE89.

findings.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) described a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy caused by biallelic GAD1 variants. It was marked by seizures starting in early infancy and by hypotonia, with variable non-CNS features such as skeletal abnormalities, dysmorphic features and cleft palate.
quotes: Here we present six affected individuals from six unrelated families, carrying bi-allelic GAD1 variants, presenting with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, characterized by early-infantile onset epilepsy and hypotonia with additional variable non-CNS manifestations such as skeletal abnormalities, dysmorphic features and cleft palate.

findings.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) reported 6 patients (3 male, 3 female) from 6 unrelated families of Persian, Pakistani, African American, Sudanese, Egyptian and Turkish ancestry; 4 of the families were consanguineous. Seizures began between 2 and 6 months of age. They were mainly focal motor seizures, with some patients also having epileptic spasms, focal non-motor seizures or bilateral motor seizures. Seizures were controlled with medication in 3 patients and were drug-resistant in 3. At seizure onset, EEG showed burst suppression in 2 patients, diffuse slowing with multifocal and generalized sharp waves in 2, and hypsarrhythmia in 2. Brain MRI was normal in all but 2 patients: 1 had slight ventricular enlargement and 1 had moderate global atrophy.
quotes: A key clinical feature common to all affected individuals was early onset seizures (from 2 to 6 months), predominantly focal motor seizures with and without impaired awareness (two with additional epileptic spasms, four with focal non-motor seizures, and five with bilateral motor seizures).
Seizures were pharmacologically controlled in three of six affected individuals, with three reported as drug-resistant.
EEG at seizure onset showed a burst suppression pattern in two individuals, diffuse slowing with multifocal as well as generalized sharp waves in two, and hypsarrhythmia in two.
findings.population: Persian, Pakistani, African American, Sudanese, Egyptian, Turkish

findings.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) found severe developmental delay in all patients. Most never developed speech or non-verbal communication, and intellectual disability was severe in 5 patients and moderate in 1. Five of 6 patients had reduced muscle strength or tone: 4 lacked head control or could not sit or crawl, and 2 depended on a nasogastric tube because of dysphagia. Mild facial dysmorphism was seen in 4 patients, and 1 had cleft palate. Other features without a common pattern included hirsutism, kidney stones, urogenital malformations, diastasis recti, reduced head circumference, clinodactyly, short arms, arthrogryposis of the lower limbs, congenital hip dislocation, high myopia and hearing impairment. Metabolic workups were normal.
quotes: Most patients did not achieve any speech or non-verbal communication, only one was reported to have developed simple speech and basic perceptive language skills.

The third key feature we observed was a reduced muscle strength (five of six individuals) of varying severity ranging from slight muscle tone (one of five) to limited head control, inability to sit or crawl (four of six) and nasogastric tube dependence, due to dysphagia (two of six).

Other features that were observed without clear common elements included hirsutism, kidney stones, urogenital malformations, diastasis recti, reduced head circumference, clinodactyly, short arms, arthrogryposis of the lower limbs and congenital hip dislocation. Metabolic workups did not show any abnormalities.

findings.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) noted that cognitive development did not improve even when seizures were controlled: although 3 of 6 patients became seizure-free, all had severe intellectual disability. The authors hypothesized that GAD1 variants affect development independently of seizure control.
quotes: However, despite seizure control (seizure freedom achieved in three of six individuals), all patients described here still showed severe intellectual disability.
We therefore hypothesize that GAD1 mutations may also play an important role in intellectual development.

findings.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) described one Egyptian patient (Family E, patient III-3), the child of first-cousin parents, who was the only patient born with cleft palate. She also had congenital bilateral hip dislocation with a shallow acetabulum, talipes equinovarus, hearing impairment, severe hypotonia and global brain atrophy. A similarly affected sibling died without genetic testing.
quotes: only one of our patients (Family E, Patient III-3) was born with a cleft palate (the same patient also showed congenital bilateral hip dislocation with shallow acetabulum, talipes equinovarus and hearing impairment.)
one similarly affected sibling passed away without any genetic testing being performed

findings.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) found that the GAD1 variants segregated with disease according to autosomal recessive inheritance, confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Variants were homozygous in 5 families and compound heterozygous in 1.
quotes: The segregation of the variants with the clinical phenotype was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, which showed a recessive mode of inheritance.
Homozygous variants were identified in five families (Families A, B, D, E and F), whereas compound heterozygous variants were found in Family C (Table 2).

findings.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous c.1691A>G (p.Asn564Ser) missense variant in GAD1 in a Persian girl (Family A) born to double-first-cousin parents. Her phenotype was relatively mild: moderate intellectual disability, simple speech, and seizures that became controlled. The variant was seen once in the heterozygous state in gnomAD, had a CADD score of 26.1 and was predicted pathogenic by SIFT, MutationTaster and PolyPhen-2. It lies in the C-terminal catalytic domain, and in silico analysis predicted reduced protein stability.
quotes: The affected proband from Family A carried a homozygous c.1691A>G, p.(Asn564Ser) variant, which is reported only once in the heterozygous state in gnomAD.
Further in silico analysis predicted a reduction in protein stability for p.(Phe324Cys) and p.(Asn564Ser)

findings.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.971T>G (p.Phe324Cys) missense variant in GAD1 in a Pakistani boy from a consanguineous family (Family B). The variant had a gnomAD minor allele frequency of 0.00000796 (2 heterozygotes) and a CADD score of 28, and all prediction tools rated it damaging. It lies in the PLP-binding domain, and in silico analysis predicted reduced protein stability.
quotes: The proband from Family B harboured a homozygous c.971T>G, p.(Phe324Cys) variant, which causes the substitution of a phenylalanine residue at position 324 with cysteine.
This variant has been seen in the heterozygous state in gnomAD with a minor allele frequency of 0.00000796. It has a CADD score of 28 and is predicted damaging by all the prediction tools used

findings.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.1040C>T (p.Thr347Met) missense variant in GAD1 in a Sudanese boy whose parents were second cousins (Family D). He had epileptic spasms with hypsarrhythmia, severe hypotonia and severe dysmorphic features. The variant had been reported twice in the heterozygous state in gnomAD and had a CADD score of 29.1. In silico analysis predicted that it breaks H-bonds in the PLP-binding domain. A heterozygous sister had a different neurodevelopmental condition without seizures.
quotes: The proband from Family D carried a homozygous c.1040C>T, p.(Thr347Met) variant, which was reported twice in the heterozygous state in the gnomAD database.
in association with a break in H-bonds in the pyridoxal 5′-phosphate (PLP) binding domain for p.(Thr347Met)
His sister (Patient II-2) is heterozygous for the same variant and suffers from a different neurodevelopmental condition without seizures.

findings.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.87C>G (p.Tyr29Ter) nonsense variant in GAD1 in an Egyptian patient whose parents were first cousins (Family E). The variant was absent from all queried population databases and had a CADD score of 35. The authors predicted that it causes nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and complete loss of function.
quotes: In Family E, a homozygous stop gain variant c.87C>G, p.(Tyr29Ter) was identified. This variant is absent in all the queried population datasets.
This null variant likely causes a nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), leading to a complete loss-of-function.

findings.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.568delC (p.Gln190SerfsTer11) frameshift variant in GAD1 in a Turkish patient whose parents were first cousins (Family F); both parents were heterozygous carriers. The variant was absent from gnomAD and the other population databases queried, and was classified as pathogenic under ACMG guidelines.
quotes: The proband from Family F carries a homozygous c.568delC p.(Gln190SerfsTer11) variant, which is absent in gnomAD and other population datasets queried.
His parents are both heterozygous carriers of the same variant.

findings.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) identified compound heterozygous GAD1 variants in an African American boy (Family C) whose parents were not reported as consanguineous: a c.1591C>T (p.Arg531Ter) nonsense variant (CADD score 43, reported only in the heterozygous state in gnomAD) and a c.670delC (p.Leu224SerfsTer5) frameshift variant. His mother carried c.670delC; his father was not available for testing.
quotes: Family C was the only family in which heterozygous variants were found: c.1591C>T, p.(Arg531*) and c.670delC, p.(Leu224Serfs*5). This individual’s mother was a carrier for c.670delC; however, the individual’s father was not available for genetic testing.

findings.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) concluded that the phenotype probably results from loss of function. They based this on four null variants, missense variants located in the PLP-binding and C-terminal catalytic domains, and the moderate intolerance of GAD1 to loss-of-function variation. They suggested that reduced GABA synthesis disrupts the balance of GABAergic signaling and so predisposes to seizures.
quotes: The likely negative impact of the missense variants on PLP-binding and C-terminal catalytic domains, together with the finding of four null pathogenic variants in our case series, supports the idea that the clinical phenotypes observed are likely due to a loss-of-function mechanism.
Since GAD1 is centrally involved in the production of GABA, GAD1 mutations likely lead to an imbalance of GABA in the brain.

relevance_reason: This paper first describes DEE caused by biallelic GAD1 variants. It reports 11 patients from 6 consanguineous families, with their variants, segregation and functional or in silico studies.

findings.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) reported 11 patients from 6 unrelated consanguineous families (Algerian, Egyptian, Turkish, Iranian, Brazilian) with a syndromic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. Seizures began in the first 2 months of life in all patients, mainly as epileptic spasms or myoclonic seizures, and early EEG showed suppression-burst, burst attenuation or hypsarrhythmia. Eight patients had joint contractures and/or pes equinovarus, 7 had cleft palate and 2 had omphalocele. All living patients had profound psychomotor delay, and 4 died before 4 years of age.
quotes: Seizure onset occurred in the first 2 months of life in all patients. All 10 patients, from whom early disease history was available, presented with seizure onset in the first month of life, mainly consisting of epileptic spasms or myoclonic seizures.

Eight patients had joint contractures and/or pes equinovarus. Seven patients presented a cleft palate and two also had an omphalocele, reproducing the phenotype of the knockout Gad1-/- mouse model. Four patients died before 4 years of age.
Interestingly, in addition to neurological features, seven patients presented a cleft palate, six joint contractures and five pes equinovarus. Scoliosis was reported in four patients.

findings.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) described 2 sibs (a boy and a girl) born to Algerian first-cousin parents (Family A). Both had cleft soft palate. The boy had developmental regression, axial hypotonia and hypsarrhythmia by 5 months of age and progressed to spastic tetraparesis with no speech at 6 years. His sister had spasms from 2 days of age with a suppression-burst EEG; seizures were controlled by 3 months with levetiracetam and vigabatrin, but she had severe developmental delay with axial hypotonia.
quotes: Case 1 was a 6-year-old male, the first child of healthy first cousin parents of Algerian origin (Fig. 1A).

When first referred to the neuropaediatric unit, at 5 months of age, the patient had developmental regression with loss of visual contact, abnormal neurological examination with opisthotonous and axial hypotonia.

The patient was admitted at 2 days of age to neonatal intensive care unit due to episodes with eye revulsion, cyanosis and spasms-like movements. EEG showed a suppression-burst pattern (Fig. 3B and C).

findings.statement: In 2 affected sibs from a consanguineous Algerian family (Family A), Chatron et al. (2020) found a homozygous splice site variant in GAD1, c.1414-1G>C, by exome sequencing. The variant was confirmed by Sanger sequencing and segregated with the disease. cDNA analysis of parental lymphoblastoid cells showed no normal mRNA from the mutant allele and 3 aberrant isoforms: one skipping exon 15, one retaining 76 bases of intron 14, and one lacking the first 7 bases of exon 15.
quotes: The c.1414-1G>C variant in Family A was predicted to abolish the acceptor splice-site of GAD1 exon 15 by in silico splicing programmes (MaxEntScan and GeneSplicer).

cDNA analysis confirmed the absence of normal mRNA product with three aberrant isoforms: one with exon 15 skipped, one with 76 bases of intron 14 retained and one with the first seven bases of exon 15 deleted.

findings.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) described a sister and brother born to Egyptian first-cousin parents (Family B). Both had omphalocele, talipes equinovarus and arthrogryposis and developed epileptic spasms and eye twitches at 2 weeks of age. Both became seizure-free on vigabatrin. The girl also had cleft soft palate, jejunal atresia, multiple dysmorphic features, hypoplastic corpus callosum, cerebral atrophy and scoliosis. The girl died at 2 years and the boy at 4 years.
quotes: Examination at birth showed omphalocele and cleft soft palate.

Seizures were first noted at 2 weeks of age in the form of eye twitches and epileptic spasms. She was treated with phenobarbital, valproic acid, oxcarbazepine, and eventually became seizure-free with vigabatrin at the age of 9 months.
Case 4 was a similarly affected brother, who passed away at the age of 4 years due to pulmonary infection and severe growth retardation.

findings.statement: In the affected sibs of Egyptian Family B, Chatron et al. (2020) identified a homozygous 3-bp deletion in exon 7 of GAD1, c.695_697delAGA, which deletes a highly conserved lysine (p.Lys232del; reported as p.Lys231del in the table). The variant was absent from public databases, and in silico tools predicted that it disrupts splicing. In a cell-free assay, the mutant protein was expressed at levels comparable to wild type. The authors noted that this assay bypasses splicing and could not formally demonstrate loss of function, but considered the variant pathogenic given the phenotype.
quotes: The proband of Family B carried a novel homozygous 3-bp deletion in exon 7, c.695_697delAGA (Fig. 1B and Supplementary Fig. 1B), leading to the deletion of a highly conserved lysine at position 232, p.(Lys232del) (Supplementary Fig. 2A).

Western blotting of wild-type and p.Lys232del-GAD67, however, revealed that p.Lys232del-GAD67 was expressed at a comparable level as wild-type-GAD67, which is not in favour of an effect on splicing (Supplementary Fig. 3).
The variant is not present in any public databases [1000 Genome Project Database, Greater Middle East (GME), ExAC/GnomAD browsers].

findings.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) described a sister and brother born to Turkish first-cousin parents (Family C). Both had cleft palate and refractory epilepsy that began in the neonatal period with myoclonic seizures and a suppression-burst EEG. Brain MRI was normal in both. The 12-year-old sister had profound intellectual disability, tetraparesis, talipes, conductive hearing loss and photosensitivity. The brother died of refractory seizures at 2 years of age.
quotes: She had an onset of eyelid-myoclonia at the age of 2 weeks, and 1 week later also showed myoclonic seizures of the upper limbs.
She has a palatine cleft, a talipes on the left side and a conductive hearing loss.
Seizures deteriorated under ketogenic diet and he died from refractory seizures at the age of 2 years.

findings.statement: In the affected sibs of Turkish Family C, Chatron et al. (2020) used whole-genome sequencing to identify a homozygous 5-bp deletion in GAD1, c.812_816delTTAAG, which causes a frameshift (p.Val271AspfsTer9). Sanger sequencing confirmed that the variant segregated with the disease.
quotes: In Family C, a homozygous 5-bp deletion, c.812_816delTTAAG, leading to a frameshift p.(Val271Aspfs*9) was identified (Fig. 1C and Supplementary Fig. 1C).

findings.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) described 2 sibs from an Iranian second-cousin family (Family D) with myoclonic seizures and epileptic spasms beginning in the first week of life and profound developmental delay. Neither had cleft palate, joint contractures or pes equinovarus. They also described 2 brothers from a Turkish first-cousin family (Family E). The older brother had cleft palate, Hirschsprung disease, pes equinovarus, flexion contractures, facial dysmorphism and hypsarrhythmia, with epileptic spasms from 1 month of age. His brother, born at 29 weeks, had cleft palate, myoclonic seizures, congenital heart disease and pes equinovarus and died on day 9.
quotes: First myoclonic seizures were noted within 1 day after birth and EEG showed dysrhythmia. The seizures evolved into epileptic spasms.

He was referred to Istanbul University Cerrahpasa Medical Faculty, Pediatric Genetic Department at 2 months of age due to facial dysmorphism, development delay, cleft palate, Hirschsprung disease, and pes equinovarus deformity (Fig. 2).

Case 10 (Patient E-III:1), the first child of the parents of proband Case 9, was born at 29 weeks of gestation, had cleft palate, short neck, narrow thorax, myoclonic seizures, congenital heart disease

findings.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) identified the same homozygous nonsense variant in GAD1, c.1591C>T (p.Arg531Ter), in Persian Family D and Turkish Family E. They suggested that a common haplotype was possible given the families' relative geographic proximity.
quotes: Families D and E, of Persian and Turkish origin, respectively, shared the same GAD1 c.1591C>T variant leading to a premature stop codon p.(Arg531*) (Fig. 1D and E and Supplementary Fig. 1D and E). Given the relative geographical proximity, a common haplotype is possible.

findings.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) described a 7-year-old girl born to Brazilian first-cousin parents (Family F). Facial twitches began at 7 days of age, and EEG showed suppression-burst. Her seizures were refractory until vigabatrin was started at 11 months of age. She had profound developmental delay, choreoathetotic movements, spasticity of the lower limbs, severe scoliosis, and cerebral atrophy with ventricular dilation. She had no cleft palate and no dysmorphic facial features.
quotes: Case 11 was a 7-year-old female, the first child of healthy first-cousin Brazilian parents of Caucasian and African ancestry.
Finally, at 11 months of age she started vigabatrin (max dose of 1000 mg), which completely controlled the seizures after 2 weeks later.
She kept her hands fisted with flexion of wrists and her arms movements were uncoordinated and choreathetotic.

findings.statement: In the Brazilian patient (Family F), Chatron et al. (2020) identified a homozygous missense variant in GAD1, c.1525G>A (p.Glu509Lys). The variant was absent from gnomAD and affects an extremely well-conserved residue in the pyridoxal-dependent decarboxylase domain. Structural modeling predicted that it disrupts salt bridges with Arg316, Lys318 and Lys389 and no longer fits into the domain core.
quotes: In Family F, another homozygous missense variant was identified, p.(Glu509Lys) (Supplementary Fig. 1F), which is absent from the gnomAD database.
The wild-type glutamate residue is predicted to form salt bridges with the arginine at position 316, the lysine at position 318 and the lysine at position 389.

findings.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) found that the GAD1 variants segregated with the disease in all families in a manner consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. Four of the 6 families carried truncating variants, which supports a loss-of-function mechanism. They also noted that GAD1 has a gnomAD pRec score of 0.934.
quotes: In all families, Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation of the GAD1 variants with the disease phenotype (Supplementary Fig. 1) and a recessive mode of inheritance associated with the disease.
as the pRec score (Lek et al., 2016) (probability of being intolerant to bi-allelic loss-of-function variants) is 0.934, above the 0.9 threshold to consider a gene intolerant to bi-allelic variants.

findings.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) suggested that the non-neural features (cleft palate, omphalocele, pes equinovarus and joint contractures) are secondary to reduced fetal movement caused by severe CNS involvement, as described in Gad1-null mice. They noted that biallelic loss-of-function variants in humans fully reproduce the combination of epilepsy, cleft palate and omphalocele seen in animal models.
quotes: As such, the non-neural phenotypes seen in our cohort of patients should probably be seen as secondary to the severe CNS involvement.
Bi-allelic loss-of-function variants in humans fully recapitulate the association of epilepsy, cleft palate and omphalocele observed in animal models.

findings.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) noted phenotypic variability between Families D and E, which carry the same variant: Family D lacked pes equinovarus, joint contractures and cleft. They suggested that genetic background or environmental factors affecting movement in utero might explain this difference.
quotes: Despite identical mutation in Families D and E, there was some phenotypic variability between both families; in particular there was an absence of pes equinovarus, joint contractures and cleft lip in Family D.

findings.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) observed a remarkably good seizure response to vigabatrin in 5 of 7 treated patients. They cautioned that the response may reflect seizure type, since epileptic spasms respond well to vigabatrin whatever the cause, and called for validation of vigabatrin as a targeted treatment.
quotes: Finally, a remarkably good response of seizures to vigabatrin was seen in five of seven individuals who were treated with the drug.
It should be noted however, that this good response seems to be driven by seizure semiology, as particularly patients with epileptic spasms appeared to benefit from vigabatrin.

relevance_reason: Mouse knockout model of Gad1 (GAD67), the gene underlying DEE89; it supplies animal model evidence (cleft palate, reduced brain GABA).

findings.statement: Asada et al. (1997) generated mice lacking GAD67 by gene targeting. Gad67 -/- mice were born at the expected frequency but died of severe cleft palate during the first morning after birth. In the cerebral cortex of newborn Gad67 -/- mice, GAD activity was reduced to 20% and GABA content to 7%, but the brain showed no discernible defects. The authors concluded that this was the first demonstration of a role for GAD67-derived GABA in the development of nonneural tissue.
quotes: These mice were born at the expected frequency but died of severe cleft palate during the first morning after birth.
GAD activities and GABA contents were reduced to 20% and 7%, respectively, in the cerebral cortex of the newborn GAD67 -/- mice. Their brain, however, did not show any discernible defects.
this is the first demonstration of a role for GAD67-derived GABA in the development of nonneural tissue

findings.statement: Asada et al. (1997) noted that, in contrast, their earlier GAD65 -/- mice showed no change in brain GABA content or behavior apart from a slight increase in susceptibility to seizures.
quotes: Recently we have produced GAD65 -/- mice and demonstrated that lack of GAD65 does not change brain GABA contents or animal behavior, except for a slight increase in susceptibility to seizures.
